lesson.title: Test and pitch it
lesson.subtitle: Test on paper, explain it, pitch it in two minutes

video.title: Test and pitch it
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds, one recurring teacher character. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Dr Farah Rahman — teacher educator from Bangladesh, visiting the school’s AI club (main character)
Mr Okafor — science teacher who runs the school’s AI club (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer, speaking to the student)

chapters.label: Models you can explain, and the lab

scenes.visual: A market stall. Two students from the AI club hold up paper phone screens drawn in marker. An older woman squints at the tiny drawn buttons, shakes her head, then points to her mouth: she wants to speak. The students look at each other, then start drawing a big microphone button. Dr Farah tells the story to the club, smiling.
scenes.animation: Paper screens flip up (200 ms); the small buttons blur; a big microphone button is drawn in one stroke.
scenes.narration: Last week, a team from your club tested a paper version of their helper with a grandmother at the market. She couldn’t read the small buttons, so she asked to speak instead. That one test changed their design.

scenes.visual: Paper-grey card. The Darsi mark pops in, then the course name, the lesson title and a yellow ‘AI’ track chip with the spark icon.
scenes.animation: Mark scales 0→100% with a small overshoot (≤ 200 ms); title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: test with real people, explain how it decides, and pitch in two minutes.

scenes.visual: A desk with paper, scissors and markers. Phone-sized paper screens are drawn and cut out. One student holds the screens as ‘the AI’ and swaps them as a friend taps; the student playing the AI keeps a straight face and says nothing when the friend hesitates.
scenes.animation: Screens are drawn with quick marker strokes; the ‘AI’ student swaps screens with a soft paper flick.
scenes.narration: You don’t need code to test an idea. Draw each screen on paper. A friend plays the user, and you play the AI, answering as your design would. Watch where they get stuck, and don’t help or explain.

scenes.visual: Three short rounds as a loop: a student tests the paper helper with a classmate, a parent, then the school secretary. After each round, sticky notes of ‘what confused them’ go up, a screen is redrawn, and the next round goes more smoothly.
scenes.animation: A loop arrow turns three times; sticky notes pile up, then fewer each round.
scenes.narration: Test with the people who’ll really use it: students, parents, the school office. Write down what confused them, change the design, and test again. Three short rounds teach you more than a month of guessing.

scenes.visual: A parent looks at the helper on a phone. A speech bubble full of jargon (‘ranking algorithm’) makes her frown. It is replaced by a plain bubble: ‘It finds the school document closest to your question, and shows it to you’, with the document’s title underneath, and she nods. A small ‘how sure’ meter appears beside the answer.
scenes.animation: The jargon bubble crumples and drops; the plain bubble slides in; the meter fills to about three quarters.
scenes.narration: People trust what they can understand. So explain how your AI decides, in your users’ words. Not “it runs a ranking algorithm”, but “it finds the document closest to your question, and shows it”. And say how sure it is.

scenes.visual: Clean white card with the AI track chip and a two-minute timer. Five rows build: the problem and its users, the data, how it works, the risks (in red), and why it can be trusted (in green).
scenes.animation: The timer ring starts; rows slide in as each part is named.
scenes.narration: So, a pitch is a two-minute story that helps people trust your idea. It covers the problem, the users, the data, how it works, the risks, and why it can be trusted.

scenes.visual: A small radio on a kitchen shelf. First it says only ‘Rain tomorrow’, and a farmer shrugs. Then it says ‘A seventy percent chance of rain, because clouds are building over the hills’; the farmer looks at the hills, nods, and covers the drying maize. Dr Farah stands at the side of the frame.
scenes.animation: Radio sound waves pulse; clouds roll over the hills; a tarpaulin is pulled over the maize.
scenes.narration: Think of a weather forecast. “Rain tomorrow” is easy to ignore. “Seventy percent chance of rain: clouds are building over the hills” is easier to trust and plan around. Explain your AI that way: what, why, how sure.

scenes.visual: Mr Okafor pops in beside the paper prototype, where a user’s finger hovers, unsure. Three answer cards drop in below him.
scenes.animation: Character slides in from the side; answer cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.on_screen_text: The user is stuck. Now what?
scenes.narration: Quick check! During a test, the user gets stuck on your paper prototype. What should you do?

scenes.visual: The card ‘Watch, take notes, change it later’ gets a check badge. A student’s notebook fills with notes: ‘stuck on screen 2’, ‘didn’t see the back button’. A ghost of the student reaching to explain is crossed out.
scenes.animation: Check badge pops (150 ms); notes write themselves; the crossed-out ghost fades.
scenes.on_screen_text: Where they stop is your data
scenes.narration: Watch, take notes, and change it later. If you explain during the test, you hide the problem: real users won’t have you there. Where they get stuck is your most useful data.

scenes.visual: Left: a simple tree of yes/no questions drawn on the board, with a finger tracing one path from top to bottom. Right: a huge tangle of connected dots labelled ‘big model’ next to a chatbot window; beside it, a source card, a ‘how sure’ meter and a test checklist appear.
scenes.animation: The finger traces the path (800 ms); the tangle pulses once; the source card, meter and checklist pop in.
scenes.narration: Some AI is easy to explain. A decision tree is a chain of questions you can follow to see exactly why it decided. Big models, like chatbots, are much harder. So show their sources, say they can be wrong, and test more.

scenes.visual: A phone screen with the ‘Decision tree’ lab: a table of fourteen days (sky, temperature, humidity, wind, played or not). A finger picks ‘What is the sky like?’, which has the biggest gain; the days split into sunny, cloudy and rainy. Under ‘sunny’, ‘How humid is it?’ splits again, and the leaf reads ‘Stay inside’.
scenes.animation: Branches grow from the top (400 ms each); the matching rows in the table light up as each branch is chosen.
scenes.on_screen_text: App lab: grow a decision tree
scenes.narration: In the app, build a decision tree from fourteen school days: the weather, and whether the class played football at break. Each question sorts the days. Then explain any decision in one sentence: sunny and humid, so we stay inside.

scenes.visual: Dr Farah beside a two-minute timer. Two answer cards appear beside her.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.on_screen_text: What builds trust in a pitch?
scenes.narration: Your turn. You have two minutes to pitch. Which of these belongs in a pitch people can trust?

scenes.visual: The ‘The risks, and how you’ll handle them’ card gets the check badge, then the screen resolves into a summary: paper screens with sticky notes, a plain-words speech bubble, and a two-minute timer.
scenes.animation: Points tick in one by one; the takeaway bar rises last.
scenes.narration: The risks, and how you’ll handle them: honesty about what could go wrong builds trust. Remember: test on paper with real users, then change it and retest. Explain how it decides, in your users’ words. And pitch the problem, users, data, how it works, risks and trust.

scenes.visual: The AI club meeting: a student stands with paper screens and a phone timer showing 2:00, pitching to the club, while Mr Okafor and classmates write questions on sticky notes. At home, the same student pitches to a parent and a grandmother. Dr Farah smiles at the side.
scenes.animation: The timer counts down; three sticky notes with question marks land on the board; end card fades in.
scenes.narration: Try it yourself: pitch your solution in two minutes to your class, your family or the AI club. Collect three questions people ask you. Then use them to improve your design.

checkpoints.prompt: During a test, the user gets stuck on your paper prototype. What should you do?

options.text: Watch, take notes, change it later
Explain how it works to them
Find a user who understands it

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — where users get stuck shows you what to change. Real users won’t have you there to explain.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — if you explain during the test, you hide the problem. Watch, take notes, and change the design afterwards.

checkpoints.prompt: Which of these belongs in a pitch people can trust?

options.text: The risks, and how you’ll handle them

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — naming the risks, and your plan for them, shows you’ve thought it through. That builds trust.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — a pitch that hides the risks is harder to trust. Say what could go wrong, and how you’ll handle it.
